title: Stack & Queue
html:
Stack & Queue

Two restrictions on access order, and the restriction is the point: it makes certain problems trivial that are awkward with random access.

Stack - last in, first out

Backed by an array (fast, contiguous) or a list. Push, pop, peek, all O(1).

Where it earns its place:

Matching pairs. Brackets, tags, quotes. Push openers, pop on a closer and check it matches. Non-empty at the end means something was never closed. Nothing else expresses nesting this cleanly.

Undoing. The natural structure for "reverse the last thing" - editor history, transaction rollback.

Turning recursion into iteration. Any recursive traversal can be written with an explicit stack. Sometimes necessary: deep recursion overflows the call stack, and an explicit stack lives on the heap where you control the size.

Monotonic stack. The one worth real study. Keep the stack sorted - popping anything that violates the order as you push. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so a whole class of "next greater element", "largest rectangle", "span until a warmer day" problems collapses from O(n²) to O(n). The insight: when you pop an element, the thing that popped it is its answer.

Queue - first in, first out

Enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front, both O(1) with the right backing. Implemented as a ring buffer over an array, or a list with head and tail.

Where it earns its place:

Breadth-first traversal. A queue explores level by level, which is why it finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph and a stack does not. Swap the queue for a stack and the same code becomes depth-first - the data structure is the traversal order.

Buffering between producer and consumer. Work arriving faster than it is handled. The queue's depth is your early warning: a queue that only grows means the consumer is too slow, and no amount of retry logic fixes that.

Deque. Both ends. Needed for a sliding-window maximum, where you push on the right, discard from the right anything smaller than the incoming value, and discard from the left anything that has fallen out of the window.

Priority queue is a different thing

Despite the name, not FIFO - it dequeues the smallest (or largest). Backed by a heap, so O(log n) push and pop, O(1) peek. Reach for it when "what is the current best" is asked repeatedly while the contents change.

Common mistakes

  • Popping an empty stack. Check, or use a form that returns a failure rather than throwing.
  • Using a list as a queue and removing from the front - that is O(n) per dequeue and turns a loop quadratic.
  • Reaching for BFS when the graph is weighted; it gives fewest edges, not lowest cost.
  • Building a monotonic stack that stores values when it needed to store indices, then being unable to compute widths.
